procedures.procedure: Office visit, established patient, moderate MDM

documents.title: Follow-up Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Follow-up after the December admission. Drew the BMP at the start of the visit and it came back this evening: creatinine 0.9, back at his baseline. Both rhabdo episodes now resolved by labs; off the active list.

Interval: back at work since late December, mostly indoor framing this winter. No weakness, no dark urine. He describes one binge over the holidays, "smaller than usual," and says he has stayed away from cocaine since December. Did not want to talk about opioids. Pack a day.

Exam: vitals as charted. Well appearing. Strength full, no muscle tenderness. Heart regular, lungs clear.

A/P
1. Recurrent rhabdomyolysis with AKI, resolved. Reviewed warning signs again.
2. AUD severe, cocaine use disorder, OUD. Asked again about medication or a program. Still no. Respecting that, and I said I will keep asking.
3. Tobacco. Advised quitting. Not ready.

RTC April, physical in May.

documents.title: Kidney test
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Declan, your kidney function from yesterday is 0.9, completely back to normal for you. Potassium normal too. Nothing to change. See you in April.

documents.title: No-show
documents.author: front desk
documents.body: Pt did not arrive for 3:40 appt. Called cell, voicemail full. Sent portal message asking him to reschedule; physical in May still on the books.

social.value: Binge drinking, 10-15 drinks per day during episodes

documents.title: Annual Physical
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
33M here for a physical. Missed April; says his phone was off for a week.

No complaints. Working full time, outside again now that it is spring. Sleep okay. Mood "fine," a bit worn down. PHQ-9 6, no thoughts of self-harm. AUDIT-C 10. Binges roughly every few weeks, same 10-15 drinks a day for a couple of days. He admits cocaine came back with the last one. Denies opioids. Pack a day, no change.

Meds: none. Allergies: NKDA.
FH unchanged: father AUD, maternal uncle OUD, mother depression.
SH: same apartment, still on his own.

Vaccines: Tdap 2024, hep B series done, PCV20 done, flu last fall. Declines COVID vaccine.

Exam: vitals as charted, BP normal, weight up a little. Well appearing. HEENT unremarkable. Neck supple, no nodes or thyroid enlargement. Heart regular without murmur. Lungs clear, no wheeze. Abdomen soft, no tenderness, liver not enlarged. Extremities without edema, full strength. Skin clear, no track marks. Affect appropriate.

A/P
1. Health maintenance. CMP, CBC, lipids today. No colon or lung screening due at his age.
2. AUD severe, cocaine use disorder, OUD. Same conversation, same answer. He knows the options. I asked him to keep the mood question open with me given his mother's history.
3. Tobacco. Advised to quit.

RTC 3-4 months.

documents.title: Physical labs
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Hi Declan, everything from your physical came back normal: kidneys, liver tests, sugar, blood counts and cholesterol. Good to see you yesterday.

documents.title: Emergency Department Provider Note (outside record)
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
Regional hospital emergency department. Date of service 10/09/2025.

CC: unresponsive.

HPI: 34-year-old man brought by EMS after his roommate could not wake him this morning. Per the roommate he uses heroin and may have used an unknown amount last night. Known alcohol, cocaine and opioid use disorders, with two prior admissions here for substance-related rhabdomyolysis; this looks like more of the same. History limited by mental status.

Allergies: NKDA.
PMH: rhabdomyolysis 4/2024 and 12/2024; AUD, cocaine use disorder, OUD.
Social: pack a day; binge drinker, 10-15 drinks daily when drinking; construction laborer. Lives with a roommate.
Family: father AUD, maternal uncle OUD, mother depression.

Arrival vitals: RR 8, BP 90/60, HR 55.

Exam: Drowsy, rouses to voice. Left lower leg swollen and tender, pale and cool compared with the right. Urine dark brown. Heart slow, regular. Lungs clear but shallow.

Course: naloxone 0.4 mg IV; within minutes RR 14 and he was more awake and conversant. IV isotonic fluids started at high rate. Orthopedics called for the left leg; DP and PT signals present by Doppler.

Data: Cr 3.2 (baseline 0.9). K 5.8. Ca 7.9. Phos 6.5. CK 20,000. UA blood positive, no RBCs on microscopy.

MDM: Opioid overdose with rhabdomyolysis and AKI, hyperkalemia, hypocalcemia and hyperphosphatemia. Left leg at risk for compartment syndrome, being evaluated by orthopedics. Admit to medicine for fluids, serial leg checks and monitoring for recurrent sedation.

Disposition: admit, medicine, step-down.

events.reason: Opioid overdose with rhabdomyolysis and acute kidney injury

procedures.procedure: Hospital discharge day management, 30 minutes or less

documents.title: Orthopedic Surgery Consult (outside record)
documents.author: orthopedic surgery
documents.body:
Regional hospital, orthopedic surgery consult, 10/09/2025. Asked by the ED to evaluate the left leg for compartment syndrome in a patient found down after opioid use with rhabdomyolysis.

Exam: Left leg swollen from knee to ankle, tender over the anterior and lateral compartments, pale and cool relative to the right. Sensation grossly intact on the dorsum and sole. DP and PT signals present by Doppler.

Compartment pressures, left leg: anterior 22, lateral 18, deep posterior 16, superficial posterior 14 mmHg. Diastolic BP 60, giving a difference above 30 in every compartment.

Impression: swollen left leg after prolonged lying, pressures below fasciotomy range at this time.

Plan: no fasciotomy. Elevate to heart level, avoid compression. Neurovascular checks every 2 hours by nursing, our team to re-examine tonight and in the morning; call immediately for rising pain or new numbness.

documents.title: Hospital Discharge Summary (outside record)
documents.author: hospital medicine
documents.body:
Regional hospital, inpatient medicine. Admitted 10/09/2025, discharged 10/14/2025. Copy to primary care physician.

Principal diagnosis: rhabdomyolysis after opioid overdose (heroin) with prolonged down time.
Secondary: acute kidney injury; hyperkalemia; hypocalcemia; hyperphosphatemia; opioid use disorder; alcohol use disorder; cocaine use disorder; tobacco use.

Course: Responded to a single dose of IV naloxone in the ED and did not re-sedate on monitoring. High-volume IV fluids for five days with good urine output. CK and creatinine trended down each day. Electrolytes normalized with fluids. The left leg was followed by orthopedics with serial exams; it never met criteria for fasciotomy, and the swelling and pallor were gone by hospital day 3. Walking without help at discharge.

Addiction medicine saw him on day 2. Buprenorphine-naloxone induction was offered and he declined. Overdose prevention education given; naloxone 4 mg nasal spray kit dispensed at discharge.

Discharge labs (10/14): Cr 1.3, K 4.3, Ca 8.6, Phos 4.0, CK 2,900.

Allergies: NKDA.
Discharge medications: naloxone 4 mg nasal spray, 1 spray in one nostril for suspected overdose, may repeat in 2-3 minutes.

Follow-up: PCP within one week with BMP and CK. Outpatient addiction treatment strongly recommended.

documents.title: Post-discharge Call
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Discharge summary, ortho consult and ED note received from the regional hospital this morning; routed to PCP. Reached pt at home. Left leg "almost normal," no numbness, walking fine. Urine normal color. Has the naloxone kit; his roommate knows where it is and how to use it. Booked PCP Tue 10/21 with labs, will give flu shot same day.

medications.sig: Spray 4 mg (1 spray) into one nostril for suspected opioid overdose; may repeat in 2-3 minutes in the other nostril

orders.order: Referral to outpatient addiction treatment program
orders.reason: Opioid, alcohol and cocaine use disorders after overdose

documents.title: Hospital Follow-up
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Third admission, and the first with an overdose. Records reviewed: found unresponsive by his roommate 10/9 after heroin, RR 8, woke with one dose of IV naloxone. CK 20,000, Cr 3.2, K 5.8, Ca 7.9, Phos 6.5. Left leg swollen, pale and cool; ortho measured compartment pressures and did not need to operate. Discharged 10/14 with Cr 1.3 and CK 2,900 and a naloxone kit. Declined buprenorphine in the hospital.

Today he is quieter than I have seen him. Says he did not plan to use that much and does not remember the night. Left calf sore for a week, now fine. No numbness or weakness. Urine normal. Has not used or had a drink since discharge, one week.

PHQ-9 8. Denies any intent to harm himself, and says the overdose was not on purpose; I believe him.

Exam: vitals as charted, down about 2 kg from May. Alert, cooperative. Left leg: no swelling, calf soft and nontender, skin warm and normal color, DP and PT pulses 2+, sensation and toe movement normal. Right leg the same. Heart regular, lungs clear.

A/P
1. Rhabdomyolysis with AKI, third episode, recovering. BMP, CK, phos today.
2. OUD with overdose; AUD severe; cocaine use disorder. For the first time he is asking what the next step would be. He still does not want to start buprenorphine from me today, but agreed to a referral to the outpatient addiction program, which I placed with his number and permission to call. Naloxone from the hospital added to his list; reviewed use with him again.
3. Mood. PHQ-9 up a little. Will watch at every visit.
4. Flu shot today.
5. Work note through 10/27.

RTC 2-3 months, sooner if the program wants anything from me.

documents.title: Blood work from yesterday
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Declan, the muscle enzyme is back to normal, and potassium, calcium and phosphorus are normal. Kidney function is 0.97, back near your usual. Keep up the water. The addiction program has your referral and should call you this week. Answer even if it is a number you don't know.

documents.title: Referral Closed
documents.author: MA
documents.body: Call from the outpatient addiction program intake coordinator. Three phone attempts and a letter since 10/22, no response from pt. They have closed the referral and are happy to reopen if he calls them directly. Our own call to pt today went to voicemail; left a message with their intake number. Routed to PCP.
